title: Osho on the Ego and the Empty Boat
description: What Osho taught about the ego, in plain words. Who is it that gets insulted, that needs to win, that is never satisfied? Chuang Tzu's empty boat, the Buddha refusing a gift of insults, an eagle who thought he was a chicken, an elephant tied with a thin rope, a frog who knew everything about his well, a man who carried his raft on his head, and a beggar's bowl that no king could fill. Then a meditation on being nobody.

chapters.title: Osho on the Ego and the Empty Boat

beats.say: There is a little voice in you that says I. I want. I am right. I have been insulted. I must win. You have heard it so many times, you think it is you.
Osho called it the ego. Not a thing, really. More like a knot. A knot in the rope of life, that makes the rope think it is separate.
And all our misery comes from that knot. Every quarrel, every war, every sleepless night.
Osho said: "When you are no more, only then for the first time will you be." Tonight, a few stories about that knot.

chapters.title: The Empty Boat
chapters.ref: Chuang Tzu · Osho, The Empty Boat

beats.say: Chuang Tzu says: a man is crossing a river in his boat, in the early morning mist. Suddenly another boat comes out of the fog and crashes into his.
He is furious. He stands up and shouts: you fool, watch where you are going! He is ready to fight.
And then he looks... and the other boat is empty. It has come loose from its rope and drifted down the river. There is nobody in it.
All his anger disappears. Who can you be angry with? He simply pushes the empty boat away and goes on.
Now Chuang Tzu says: if you can empty your own boat as you go over the river of the world, nobody will fight with you. Nobody will try to harm you.
Because there is nobody there to be harmed. The insults will pass through you like wind through an empty house.
Osho gave a whole series of talks on this story, The Empty Boat. This is not weakness. It is the greatest strength. The empty boat cannot be sunk.
A man came to the Buddha in a great rage. He had heard that his son had become a monk. He stood in front of the Buddha and shouted insults at him for a long time.

The Buddha sat silently, listening. When the man was finally exhausted, the Buddha asked him a question. Tell me, if you bring a gift to someone, and he does not accept it, to whom does the gift belong?
The man said: to me, of course. I brought it.
Then, said the Buddha, I do not accept your gift. Your anger is yours. Please, take it home with you.
The man stood there, his mouth open. Nobody had ever refused his anger before. And something in him broke open. He bowed down, and asked to stay.
When someone insults you, they are handing you a parcel. You don't have to open it. You don't have to carry it home.
Osho taught: the ego grabs every parcel. Awareness simply watches it being offered... and lets it stay where it came from.
A farmer found an eagle's egg in the hills and brought it home. He put it under one of his hens, and in time a little eagle hatched among the chickens.
He grew up thinking he was a chicken. He scratched in the dirt for worms. He clucked. He flapped his great wings and jumped a few feet into the air, like the others.
One day, when he was old, he saw a magnificent bird flying high above him in the blue sky, gliding on the wind without moving its wings.
What is that? he asked. That is the eagle, said the chickens. The king of the birds. He belongs to the sky. We belong to the earth. Don't even think about it.
And so the eagle lived and died as a chicken. Because that is what he thought he was.
The ego is a borrowed idea of who you are. Borrowed from your parents, your school, your neighbours. Small, frightened, scratching in the dirt.
Osho taught: drop the conditioning. You are not what they told you. You have wings. Look up. The sky has been waiting for you.

chapters.title: The Elephant and the Thin Rope

beats.say: A traveller passing through a village saw a huge elephant tied to a small wooden stick with a thin rope. The elephant could have broken it with one step. But it stood there, quietly.
He asked the elephant keeper: why does it not run away? And the keeper said: when it was a baby, we tied it with this same rope. It pulled and pulled, but it was too small to break it.
After a while it stopped trying. Now it is grown up, and strong enough to pull down a house. But it still believes the rope is stronger.
How many thin ropes are you tied with? I cannot sing. I am not intelligent. I am not the kind of person who meditates. Ropes from childhood.
The ego is made of such ropes. Ideas about yourself, tied when you were too small to say no.
Osho called these ropes conditioning. Just take one step. You will be surprised how easily they break.
A frog lived at the bottom of an old well. One day a turtle from the great eastern sea came by and looked over the edge.
Come down! said the frog. My well is the finest place in the world. I can jump on the edge, swim in the water, sit in the mud. I am the king of everything here!
The turtle tried to climb in, but its leg got stuck in the narrow opening. So it told the frog about the sea. A thousand miles wide, and so deep that nobody has found the bottom.
The frog was silent. Then it said: you are lying. Nothing can be bigger than my well.
The ego is a well. Small, and comfortable, and very sure of itself. My religion, my country, my opinions. Anything bigger feels like a lie.
Osho taught: meditation is climbing out of the well. It is frightening at first. Then you see the sky.

chapters.title: The Man Who Carried His Raft

beats.say: The Buddha told of a man who came to a wide river. There was no bridge, no boat. So he cut branches and reeds, tied them together into a raft, and floated safely to the other side.
Then he thought: this raft has been so useful to me. I will not leave it here. And he lifted it onto his head, and carried it with him through the forest, for the rest of his life.
The Buddha said: my teachings are like a raft. Use them to get over the river. Then leave them on the bank, and walk on, free.
Even spiritual things can feed the ego. I am a meditator. I am religious. I know the words of the masters by heart. Another raft on the head.
Osho taught: use a method, then drop it. Use everything. Hold nothing. Not even this.
A beggar came to a king's palace with his bowl. The king, in a good mood, said: I will fill your bowl with anything you like. The beggar said: fill it with gold.
The servants poured in gold coins, and they disappeared. More gold. It disappeared too. The king emptied his whole treasury into that small bowl, and still it was empty.
The king fell at the beggar's feet. Tell me the secret of this bowl. And the beggar laughed. There is no secret, he said. It is made from a human skull. It is the human mind.
Whatever you put into it, it is never enough. More money, more fame, more praise. The ego is a bowl without a bottom.
Osho taught: desire can never be filled, only seen through. And the moment you see it, you stop pouring.
Now sit, and close your eyes. Osho taught that the ego dissolves in watching. Let the body be still. Let the breath be easy.
Look for the one you call I. Where is it? In the head? In the chest? Look carefully, as you would look for a lost coin.
You will find thoughts. You will find feelings, sensations, memories. But the I itself... is it there? Keep looking. Don't answer with words.
Like an onion. Peel off one layer, and another, and another... and in the end, there is nothing in the middle. Only space.
Rest in that space. The boat is empty. Let the river carry it.
Nobody to defend. Nobody to prove. Nobody to become. Feel how light that is.
This emptiness is not dead. It is full of life. Birds singing, the heart beating, the whole universe breathing through you.
Now slowly come back. Take a deep breath, and open your eyes. Go into the day as an empty boat, my friend.
